questions.q: What is the purpose of a shadow rotation for a new platform engineer?
options: To let them carry the pager alone immediately so they learn faster
To let them observe an experienced on-call engineer handle real pages and triage before carrying the pager alone
To replace the need for any runbooks
To reduce the size of the primary/secondary rotation
questions.explain: Shadow rotations let a new hire see real pages, real triage, and real false alarms before they're responsible for responding alone.

questions.q: According to the PagerDuty incident-response guidance referenced in this lesson, what should happen to an alert that has no documented runbook?
options: It should page the most senior engineer instead of the on-call primary
It generally shouldn't be allowed into the paging rotation at all
It should page every member of the team simultaneously
It should be escalated directly to an SLA breach
questions.explain: If nobody can write down what a human should do when an alert fires, the alert isn't ready to wake anyone up — it should not page until a runbook exists.

questions.q: Why does a 'fast burn' alert page immediately while a 'slow burn' alert on the same error budget only opens a ticket?
options: Fast burn alerts are always false positives
The fast burn rate would exhaust the error budget in about a day or two if left unaddressed, while the slow burn rate leaves roughly a week to fix it without urgency
Slow burn alerts only apply to batch-scored models
There is no real difference; the split is arbitrary
questions.explain: Burn-rate alerting pages based on how fast the budget would be exhausted at the current rate — a fast burn needs attention now, a slow burn can become a ticket.

questions.q: Why is alert fatigue a bigger risk on ML platforms than on many typical backend services?
options: ML platforms never use runbooks
Model prediction metrics naturally shift a little every day, so alerting on raw metric wobble instead of SLO burn produces constant, meaningless pages
ML platforms don't support secondary on-call engineers
ML models cannot be monitored at all
questions.explain: Natural day-to-day drift in prediction distributions means naive metric-based alerts fire constantly on noise, training engineers to ignore pages — including the real ones.

questions.q: What is the recommended 'usefulness test' for deciding whether a paging alert should remain in the rotation?
options: Whether it has led to a real human action in the last 90 days
Whether it has ever fired even once
Whether it is tied to an SLA rather than an SLO
Whether the alert's metric name is easy to read
questions.explain: If an alert hasn't required real human action within 90 days, it should be demoted to a non-paging channel or removed — it's adding fatigue without adding value.
